user.title: What is this for?
user.description:
Both answers are fine, and you can change your mind later.

**Set up my inverter** is what you want if you came here to see your solar production in Home Assistant.

**Diagnostics only** connects to the inverter, works out what it is and what it answers, and creates **no entities at all**. It exists because this project has to *measure* which registers each model and firmware supports — Sungrow's own specification has been wrong in both directions — and today that evidence comes from four houses. Picking it skips the one irreversible question in this dialog, about which entity ids to take over, because a reading does not need it.

entity_ids.description:
Home Assistant found **{count} entities** from the `modbus_sungrow.yaml` package, such as `{example}`. Your recorder history, your statistics and every dashboard card are stored against those entity IDs.

{status}

**Migrate my existing entities** takes those IDs over. History and statistics carry on uninterrupted and your dashboards keep working unchanged. Nothing is copied and nothing is deleted.

**Start fresh** gives this inverter its own IDs, such as `sensor.sh10rt_total_dc_power`. Your old history stays where it is, under the old IDs, and your dashboards keep pointing at it.

Either way the entities are identical in every other respect.

preview_release.title: Sungrow Modbus is a preview
preview_release.description:
This integration is a preview release, for testers rather than for a system you depend on.

**Entity names may still change.** A name supplies an entity id when the entity is first created, so a change does not move the ids you already have -- your history and dashboards are safe. What it does mean is that your ids can end up differing from somebody who installs later. Where that matters, a rename will ship with a migration that moves yours across and carries the history with it.

**What is not in flux:** readings, units, and the migration from the YAML package. If you chose to keep the YAML package's entity ids, those are reproduced exactly and none of this touches them.

Please report anything that looks wrong -- that is what a preview is for.

polling.title: Polling
polling.description:
Registers are read in four groups. Each group is one request cycle, so the interval you set is how often that whole group is fetched.

{tiers}

**Why this is worth changing.** A Sungrow inverter accepts very few Modbus connections at once. If something else polls it — the YAML package, another Home Assistant, EVCC, a logger — you are competing for one, and most reported dropouts are exactly that. Slowing a group down, or switching it off, is the cheapest fix there is.

Set **0** for never: that group is not read at all and its entities are not created. The minimum otherwise is 5 seconds — Sungrow's protocol warns against polling frequently through a WiNet-S dongle, and 5 seconds is already the fastest the YAML package ever used.

Changing anything here reloads the integration.

settings.title: Battery and diagnostics
settings.description:
**Battery charge power.** {battery_status}

The maximum a battery will take is not something the inverter knows — it reports its own converter rating, but not the pack's limit. Sungrow's own technical training recommends the **rated current × the low end of the voltage range**, not the nominal voltage: being conservative here is good for the battery's health.

*Example — a Pylontech Force H1, 14.4 kWh: the datasheet gives a recommended charge current and an operating voltage range per module. Take the current × the lowest voltage in the range, not the nominal one. For a stack reporting 25 A at 355 V that is 25 × 355 ≈ 8875 W, and rounding down to 8500 W costs almost nothing.* Check your own datasheet — the arithmetic is the point, not these numbers.

Leave it at 0 to let the integration work it out.

---

**Diagnostics.** Settings → Devices & Services → Sungrow Modbus → **Download diagnostics** produces a file describing this setup: the model, which capabilities the inverter confirmed, which registers reported themselves unavailable, how each poll group is doing, and why any entity was not created. The serial number and host address are removed from it.

data.register_dump: Include a raw register dump in diagnostics

data_description.battery_max_power: 0 means work it out: a Sungrow pack is identified from the capacity it reports and looked up against its datasheet, and any other pack that reports a BMS charge current gets that instead. Set a value to override either.
data_description.register_dump: Adds every mapped register's raw value. Only useful when a value looks wrong and the decoding itself is in question. Producing it is a second full read of the register map on top of normal polling, which is slow over a WiNet-S dongle, so leave it off unless you have been asked for it.

permissions.title: Permissions
permissions.description:
**Starting and stopping the inverter** is an action rather than a switch, so this integration decides who may call it, and you decide here. Administrators only is the default: there is no way back from a stopped inverter except another call, and the house runs on the grid until somebody makes it.

Opening it to users means users who can already change this device — a read-only login still cannot, and neither setting affects automations or scripts, which act for the household rather than for a person.

**Everything else is not ours to decide, and it is worth knowing what already applies.** The settings this integration exposes — the state-of-charge limits, the EMS mode, the export and power limits — are entities, and Home Assistant checks who may control an entity itself, before any integration is asked. By default a normal user can change all of them and a read-only user none of them. To restrict one person, make their account read-only under *Settings → People*; there is no per-setting permission in Home Assistant for us to offer.

data_description.start_stop: Who may call the start and stop actions on this inverter.

external.title: Another inverter on the same supply
external.description:
This inverter works out your house load from its own production and its grid meter. A second, non-Sungrow inverter is invisible to it, so the load reading comes out **low by exactly what that inverter is making** — and negative once it makes more than the house uses.

{reported_load}

Name the entities that report the other inverter's power and this integration adds two corrected sensors. For **energy** in kWh, do not use this page: the Energy dashboard already accepts several solar sources, and adding yours there is both easier and more accurate.

One thing to check when picking a source: some integrations report `unavailable` overnight rather than 0 W. The corrected sensors then go unknown overnight too, because a generator that is not reporting is not the same as one making nothing — assuming zero would put back the very error this page removes.

data.external_sources: Power sensors for the other generation

data_description.external_sources: Only power sensors are listed. Pick every one that reports generation this Sungrow cannot see; leave empty to switch the correction off.
data_description.external_placement: This changes the arithmetic, so it is asked rather than guessed.

survey.title: Contribute a capability survey
survey.description:
Sungrow publishes no release notes, and its register specification has been wrong in both directions — so which registers your inverter answers is **measured** rather than looked up. Today that evidence comes from nine readings at four houses, all of them the maintainer's or a friend's, which is why some inverters are supported better than others.

{measured}

Everything below is optional and answers something **no register can**. Leaving a field empty is honest — it records that the question was not answered, which is different from answering "I don't know".

Then use **Download diagnostics** on this integration and attach the file to an issue. It reads and never writes, and the serial number is replaced by a stand-in before it reaches the file.

data.survey_proxy: Is a Modbus proxy in the path?
data.publish_address: May the last two octets of the address be published?

data_description.reporter: Credited in the published reading, and who gets asked if a row raises a question. Leave empty to contribute anonymously.
data_description.survey_transport: Cable against dongle is measured already. What only you know is whether a dongle is on its Ethernet socket or its WiFi — a WiNet-S answers identically either way, so "not sure" is a real answer and better than a guess.
data_description.survey_proxy: modbus-proxy, evcc's proxy, a Home Assistant add-on. A proxy holds one connection and lends it out, so it changes what a dropped register means — and it rebuilds every frame, which can hide or create the frame quirks this project tracks.
data_description.survey_pollers: This Home Assistant is recorded automatically. What matters here is anything else: another Home Assistant, the YAML package, evcc, a logger. An inverter grants very few connections, and two clients competing for one looks exactly like a broken register.
data_description.survey_battery: No register reports it. "SBR096" or "Pylontech Force H1, 14.4 kWh" is more useful than a capacity the inverter already reports.
data_description.survey_comment: Anything unusual about the installation — a cluster, a second inverter, a wallbox, a firmware update you remember.
data_description.publish_address: Off by default. Only the last two octets, and only if you say so; otherwise the reading says xxx.xxx. It lets you tell which box each of several similar readings came from.

survey_result.title: Thank you — here is what your inverter said
survey_result.description:
{found}

---

**Now send it.** The reading is not a file yet. To get one:

Settings → Devices & services → **Sungrow Modbus** → the three dots beside this entry → **Download diagnostics**. It saves a `.json` file to your browser's downloads.

Then attach that file to [a compatibility report]({issue_url}), or post it on [Discord]({discord_url}) if you would rather not use GitHub.

**What is in it:** what your inverter answered, and your answers above. **What is not:** your serial number, which is replaced by a stand-in, and your IP address unless you allowed the last two octets. Nothing was written to the inverter.

This message is also waiting for you under Notifications, so you do not have to remember the menu path.

survey_failed.title: The reading did not complete
survey_failed.description:
Your answers will still be saved, so nothing is wasted.

The inverter stopped answering partway through:

```
{error}
```

That is worth reporting in itself — a link that cannot complete 24 reads is a finding. A Sungrow accepts very few connections at once, so the most common cause is something else polling it: another Home Assistant, the YAML package, evcc, or a logger. Try again in a minute, or slow the polling down under Options → Polling.

start_inverter.description: Boots an inverter that has been shut down. Deliberately an action rather than a button: Home Assistant has no confirmation dialog for a button press, and admin rights are required to call this.

stop_inverter.name: Stop inverter
stop_inverter.description: Shuts the inverter down. It stops generating, stops charging and stops discharging until it is started again. Deliberately an action rather than a button, and admin rights are required to call it — a dashboard card cannot do this by accident.
